brief.topic: The Coin That Looks Closer Than It Is

s01: A coin under water can look closer to the surface than it really is.
The light bringing its image to you has changed direction.
Follow two rays from the coin toward the surface.
As light leaves water for air, it bends away from the vertical normal.
Your eye traces those arriving rays backward in straight lines.
Those backward lines meet above the real coin.
That meeting point is a virtual image.
Light does not actually come from that point.
It only arrives as though it did.
The change happens at the water surface, not inside the coin.
Looking nearly straight down, the apparent depth is roughly three quarters of the real depth.
Water has a refractive index near four thirds, compared with about one for air.
The near-vertical depth ratio is the inverse of that index ratio.
A coin four units deep would look about three units deep.
This simple depth rule is an approximation for small viewing angles.
At wider angles, the geometry needs the full law of refraction.
A familiar object can stay exactly where it is, while the path of seeing changes.

scenes.narration:
A coin under water can look closer to the surface than it really is. The coin has stayed still. The light bringing its image to you has changed direction.

Follow two rays from the coin toward the surface. As light leaves water for air, it bends away from the vertical normal. Your eye traces those arriving rays backward in straight lines. Those backward lines meet above the real coin.

That meeting point is a virtual image. Light does not actually come from that point. It only arrives as though it did. The change happens at the water surface, not inside the coin.

Looking nearly straight down, the apparent depth is roughly three quarters of the real depth. Water has a refractive index near four thirds, compared with about one for air. The near-vertical depth ratio is the inverse of that index ratio. A coin four units deep would look about three units deep.

This simple depth rule is an approximation for small viewing angles. At wider angles, the geometry needs the full law of refraction. A familiar object can stay exactly where it is, while the path of seeing changes.
